html:
The Haudenosaunee, "people of the longhouse", are the Iroquoian-speaking nations of what is now upstate New York. Their land ran from the Hudson valley west to the Genesee River and Lake Erie. Europeans called them the Iroquois.

They lived in towns of bark longhouses, each shared by related families under the authority of the clan mothers. Women farmed maize, beans and squash, and men hunted, traded and made war.

Five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, joined in the Haudenosaunee Confederacy under the Great Law of Peace, likely in the 1400s. In the 1600s they used Dutch guns from the fur trade to defeat the Huron and other neighbours. The Tuscarora joined in the early 1700s, making Six Nations. See also Iroquois.
